extracted.intended_audience: prospective society editors / newspaper reporters / journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and editing society (social/personal) news, related feature stories, and for producing follow-up and rewrite stories in newspapers. Covers scope, tone, sources, typographical conventions, sample content elements, and methods for pursuing follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature sports stories (when news value is small)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual news value is small; the interest of the story lies rather in its informative worth, the writer's purpose being to present general, but significant, facts that will interest followers of the sport. Usually it is expository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in Sunday editions or when athletic news is scarce; give general surveys and background (examples: "Batters in the American Association Weaker in 1916 than in 1915"; "Ty Cobb's Place in Baseball History"). These are the feature stories of sports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of society news
rubrics_metrics.description: The society editor's work concerns itself with the social and personal news of the city and county in which the paper is published or from which it draws its patronage. It is almost entirely local.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State or out-of-city items are of value only insofar as they affect local readers through exchanges of courtesy or hospitality. Do not include the unconventional or abnormal (elopements, clandestine marriages, unusual engagements, freakish parties) in the society sphere — those belong in regular news columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: restraint, discrimination, and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The society editor must exercise consistent care, discrimination, and habitual restraint; she must recognize relative social distinctions and present details acceptably to various social groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extravagant, fawning, or gushing language (anti-pattern: overblown, flowery wedding descriptions). Equally avoid trite, colorless words and stock phrases that make copy dull. Study models showing restraint and dignity of tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and feature appropriate social names/functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor must know what names and functions to feature in her column or section and be able to present the details of those functions acceptably to the social groups about which she is writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to relative social distinctions when deciding who to name or highlight; wrong emphasis or omission can offend or misrepresent social groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content elements for engagements and wedding announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement and wedding write-ups should include the announcing persons, full names of bride and groom, parentage, addresses, affiliations (clubs, universities), attendants (maids of honor, bridesmaids, ushers), ceremony details, reception arrangements, and immediate plans (e.g., travel, residence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write succinctly but include the facts readers expect (who, where, when, who attended, dress/flowers only insofar as they are customary details). Use examples in the book as accepted methods of handling such write-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content elements for teas, dinners, luncheons, receptions, dances
rubrics_metrics.description: Social-event write-ups should describe the occasion (who gave it), notable guests/hosts, decorations and setting, noteworthy costumes or themes when relevant, and any distinctive features of the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on what makes the event newsworthy (notable attendees, unusual themes, charitable purpose). Avoid irrelevant flowery description; emphasize organization and notable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club reporting: emphasize constructive work
rubrics_metrics.description: Club news (especially women's clubs) involves literature, education, community betterment, social relief, and similar subjects and offers opportunities for constructive news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid filling the society page with dull routine; instead feature new studies and practical efforts (e.g., garbage campaigns, anti-fly work, comforts for slum children) under attractive, individual heads to engage intelligent readers and build a constructive department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personals: short personal items
rubrics_metrics.description: Include brief personal notes—returns from trips, convalescences, births, household movements, summer plans and similar items affecting local persons of prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep personals concise, accurate, and factual; they function as short notices of social mobility and life events for the readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society in prospect and review (seasonal overviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide previews and reviews of the social season — highlight state dinners, receptions, debutantes' activities, and overall social calendar patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these pieces to give readers a synthetic picture of the social season (what's happening, who is prominent, patterns of events), not merely itemized notices; this can include commentary on trends (e.g., increased dancing, changes in guest lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style for society pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Study and follow the typographical style of the society column in your paper: some papers run each affair under a separate head, others group all society stories under a general 'Society' head, indicating different functions only by new paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing lists of names, group like names/titles together: first married couples, then married women whose names appear alone, then unmarried women (Misses), and finally the men. Be aware paragraph lengths may become long under grouped styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept spurious announcements; verify sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept announcements of engagements, marriages, and births from any others than the immediate persons concerned; beware of announcements given by telephone as practical jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many newspapers use printed announcement forms mailed to families requiring signatures. Always verify announcements directly with the persons involved to avoid embarrassing errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best sources for society news and necessity of fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful sources include social leaders, friendly acquaintances in society, but especially caterers, florists, and hair-dressing parlors; these are often informed well in advance of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visit or call these places regularly to keep abreast of coming events. However, always be absolutely certain of the accuracy of addresses, names, and initials — errors can provoke immediate and severe reader complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: follow-ups vs rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: "Follow-ups" and "rewrites" are news stories which have appeared in print; the distinction is that 'follow-ups' contain news in addition to that of the story first printed, while 'rewrites' are only revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the difference when assigned a story: if new facts exist, aim for a follow-up; if not, a rewrite may merely clarify or improve the original copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive value of follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Few news stories are complete on first appearance; new features, motives, causes, and results often develop and may be of constructive value (e.g., following physicians/scientists through an epidemic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should not consider a story ended until they have run to ground its possibilities. Follow-ups that track the work of scientists, investigators, or reformers can provide greater educational and public-value reporting than sensational initial figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to follow up a story (practical steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: When handed a story to follow up: read the whole original story carefully; be familiar with the news; look to see if the reporter who wrote it played up the real features or missed the main feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for newly developed facts or human-interest angles missed initially; change of tone or focus (as in the shoplifting example) can turn an indifferent item into an engaging follow-up. Familiarity with all ongoing news is expected of newspaper people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature newly learned facts in follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: In a follow-up, the newly learned facts should be featured — e.g., funeral arrangements in sudden deaths, investigation or placing of blame in wrecks, developments in legal cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with what is new and of interest to a large body of readers; do not merely rehash earlier material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-interest and tone shifts to enrich follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: A follow-up can change tone and emphasize human-interest details (e.g., detailed personal description and background) that were absent in the initial short item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ narrative detail and character sketches judiciously to make follow-ups more compelling, while still maintaining accuracy and relevance.
